t: Why Pay-Per-Lead Sites Cost More Than They Look
d: The price on a pay-per-lead invoice is rarely the price of a job. You pay when a homeowner fills in a form, whether or not they are ready to hire and…
x: The price on a pay-per-lead invoice is rarely the price of a job. You pay when a homeowner fills in a form, whether or not they are ready to hire and whether or not you are the only contractor who receives it. The lead may be in several inboxes In many lead-sale models, one homeowner request is sent to multiple contractors at once. So the moment you pay, you are racing others to a phone the homeowner may not answer. The homeowner often filled in the form to see options, not to take a string of sales calls. That mismatch explains why so many paid leads never pick up, or already have a bid in hand and only want a price check. Cost per lead is the wrong number The number that matters is cost per job won: total lead spend divided by jobs booked. Here is an illustrative example: Step Illustrative figure Leads bought at $40 each 24 leads, $960 Leads where the homeowner answers 6 Jobs you win after competing 2 Cost per job won $480 Plug in your own numbers. If a $40 lead turns into a $480 acquisition cost, the platform’s price tag was never the real price. What contractors commonly report Contractors who have bought leads describe a familiar pattern: prices that creep up, homeowners who never answer, leads that already have bids, and homeowners surprised to be called by several companies. Some describe trouble cancelling. Regulators have also looked at the category. In January 2023 the FTC accepted a settlement with HomeAdvisor over allegations that it overstated how often its leads turned into jobs and misdescribed where some leads came from. The dispute ended in a $7.2 million settlement while the company did not admit wrongdoing ( TechCrunch ). Read the terms before you buy Before spending, ask three questions: Do you pay for leads that never answer? Can you cancel without a fee? Does the contract renew automatically? Some contractors report being locked into multi-year agreements, or getting leads for the wrong kind of job. Get the answers in writing. Keep the comparison fair, too. Google’s own Local Services Ads also charge per lead, so the same cost-per-job math applies there. Lead sites are not evil. They just should not be your only source, because you cannot control their price, their lead quality or how your reviews appear. What to do instead Work out your cost per job won for every channel, using the table above. Put effort into channels you own: a clear website, a complete Google listing and steady reviews. t: How Specializing Lets a Handyman Charge More
d: Specialists don’t compete on price. Here’s why getting really good at one or two jobs lets handymen charge more, and how bundling services adds revenue on…
x: When you are known for one thing, customers stop comparing you against the cheapest person on a TaskRabbit. They are buying certainty. You have done this exact job dozens of times, you show up with the right parts and tools, and you finish quickly. Speed is the part many new handymen miss: the faster you are, the higher the hourly rate you can earn even if the customer pays a fair flat price . Let the customer bring the materials A good way to keep your take home rate higher is by making sure the client supplies the necessary product or materials, such as a TV, a faucet, or a smart doorbell. That keeps your costs down and removes the headache of buying, returning, and marking up parts. The profit margin goes up because you are selling labor and skill, not inventory. Set expectations before you arrive Certain projects require a lot more time and can put your profit at risk. Decorative light fixtures with endless crystals can eat an afternoon, so agree beforehand who assembles them. And on a garbage disposal install with a dishwasher, knocking out the knockout plug is easy to forget (… trust us, we’ve all done it), so build it into your checklist. Small misses like these cost you a free return visit and a bit of goodwill. Bundle and offer solutions customers did not know they needed When someone books a TV mount, ask whether they want the wires hidden in the wall, and whether they would like a soundbar installed at the same time. Customers rarely think about cable runs until the TV is up and the wire is dangling. Solving a problem they did not know they had is where the extra revenue comes from , and it makes the job feel like a better experience. A reality check before you raise your rates Treat the hourly numbers as a goal, not a promise, and check your local rules first. Remember, some plumbing and electrical work may be restricted by licensing, so look up what your state or city allows before advertising swaps like faucets, disposals, or light fixtures. A simple pricing approach Pick one or two niches from the list in the previous post. Track how long each job really takes over your first ten jobs. Quote a flat price based on your fastest reliable time, plus a margin for surprises. Add an optional add-on to every quote, such as hidden wires or a second fixture. Raise your price once you are booked out for a few weeks. Premium rates need a business that answers the phone, not a voicemail box. t: The 5 Most Profitable Handyman Jobs You Can Start Offering Today
d: If you are still taking every random job that comes your way, you are probably leaving money on the table. The handymen who earn the most tend to pick a…
x: If you are still taking every random job that comes your way, you are probably leaving money on the table . The handymen who earn the most tend to pick a small set of repeatable jobs, get fast at them, and let their reputation do the marketing. Here are five of the best places to start, counted down from five to one, with tips on what makes each one pay. 5. Drywall repair Drywall is high skill but needs very little material to get started . Plenty of homeowners cannot fix a hole themselves, and plenty of homes have holes. It is hard at first, but every patch makes you faster, and once you are known as the person who makes walls disappear, referrals follow. 4. Door and lock installation Replacing doorknobs and deadbolts is simple work that many people would rather not touch. Doors are one of the things in a house that constantly break or get damaged, so demand never dries up. The tool list is short, which keeps your profit margin high, and you can become the go-to door person in your neighborhood. 3. Ceiling fans and light fixtures Most residential fans and fixtures are close to identical, so each install teaches you something that applies to the next one. One warning: a fixture the customer calls “easy” can turn out to have a thousand tiny parts, and hanging them can take hours. Settle up front who handles these intricate fixtures or price that job differently. 2. Faucets and garbage disposals The theme here is swapping, not building. Pulling out a kitchen faucet and putting in a new one is far quicker than anything that involves construction. Disposals are similar, since the problem is often a tripped breaker, a clog, or a simple replacement. 1. TV mounting and smart home installs This category is big enough that some people build whole businesses on it: TVs, soundbars, video doorbells, smart thermostats, and a growing list of connected appliances. The work is cleaner than drywall or plumbing, customers usually buy the equipment, and it feels like a specialist service. Bigger TVs may need a second person, but otherwise the barrier is low. The common thread All five jobs are fast to learn, need few tools, are easy to repeat, and often let the customer supply the materials. Pick one or two, get very good at them, and you stop competing as a generalist and start stuffing your pockets. Becoming the go-to handyman means being reachable when the phone rings, even while you’re on a ladder.
